<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but A executed the comparison-of-magnitudes burden more cleanly. A's stylized arithmetic (even discounted for worst-case escalation) gave the judge a concrete way to weigh savings against harm, and A repeatedly forced B to either quantify the alleged degradation or concede it couldn't be quantified. B's conceptual move—reframing the risk as correlated/fat-tailed rather than linear—was the debate's most original contribution and a real threat to A's arithmetic, but when directly pressed (twice) for any flip-rate or magnitude, B declined to offer one, retreating to "it needs one bad day" rather than engaging the sensitivity analysis A offered. A exploited this gap effectively in closing ("Twice, silence... an unmeasurable harm cannot be weighed against measured savings"), and also neutralized B's Klarna and Air Canada evidence by reframing them as consistent with a "most, not all" hybrid rather than counterevidence. B's governance-cost and churn arguments were substantive but stayed largely qualitative, so the debate resolves in A's favor on execution, even though B's underlying risk-framing point was conceptually strong and never fully answered on the merits.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's arithmetic in Rebuttal 1 ([A2.1]-[A2.3]), conceding B's own worst-case 25% escalation assumption and still showing a 70%+ savings collapse, was the pivotal move: it forced B to spend the rest of the debate arguing that quantification itself was the wrong frame rather than contesting the numbers directly, which A then used devastatingly in the closing by pointing to B's refusal to name any flip-rate under direct pressure questioning.</best_rebuttal>
